passages.t: The mountain goat, the wild donkey, and the wild ox
passages.happening:
“Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Have you watched the doe bear her fawn? Can you count the months they are pregnant? Do you know the time they give birth?” (verses 1-2). They crouch and bring forth their young, and the young grow strong in the open field, leave, and do not come back.

“Who set the wild donkey free? Who released the swift donkey from the harness?” (verse 5). God gave him the wilderness for his home. ‘He scorns the tumult of the city and never hears the shouts of a driver’ (verse 7).

“Will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he stay by your manger at night?” (verse 9). Can Job harness him to the plow, or trust him to bring in the grain?
passages.hearers:
God's first speech continues without a break. Chapter 38 ranged over earth, sea, sky and stars and ended with the lion and the raven. Now the focus narrows to animals, most of them wild creatures beyond human reach. The speech is still made of questions, and it still says nothing about Job's suffering or the test of the prologue.

The mountain goat is the ibex, which still lives in the rocky hills near the Dead Sea around En Gedi. The wild donkey roamed the desert fringes. The wild ox, the re'em, is usually identified with the aurochs, the great wild cattle of the ancient world, now extinct. The Greek translation rendered the word as a one-horned creature, which is why older English Bibles have unicorn.

Almost every creature here is one people cannot tame or use. People valued the tame donkey and the ox for their work. God chooses the wild ones. Their freedom is his gift, and they belong to him, not to any human master.

And notice the first picture. God watches the goats in labor and counts their months.
passages.later: The same wild donkey stands for an untamed life in Genesis: Ishmael ‘will be a wild donkey of a man’ (Genesis 16:12).
passages.asks: God counts the months of a mountain goat no one will ever see. Ask what it means to you that God watches what no one else watches. And ask whether you value creatures, and people, only for what they can do for you.

passages.t: The ostrich and the war horse
passages.happening:
‘The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork’ (verse 13). She leaves her eggs on the ground to warm in the sand, forgetting that a foot may crush them. ‘For God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not endowed her with understanding’ (verse 17). ‘Yet when she proudly spreads her wings, she laughs at the horse and its rider’ (verse 18).

“Do you give strength to the horse or adorn his neck with a mane?” (verse 19). He leaps like a locust and terrifies with his snorting. He paws the valley and charges into battle. ‘He laughs at fear, frightened of nothing; he does not turn back from the sword’ (verse 22). He cannot stand still when the ram's horn sounds, and he catches the scent of battle from far off.
passages.hearers:
The ostrich passage is humorous. The bird looks foolish: she lays her eggs in the sand and seems careless of them. Yet she outruns horse and rider. The description reflects how ostriches looked to ancient observers; modern naturalists note that ostriches tend their nests more than the poem suggests. The poem is not teaching zoology; it is delighting. God made a creature that is ridiculous and magnificent at once.

The war horse is among the most admired passages of Hebrew poetry, full of sound and motion. Horses pulled chariots and later carried mounted troops. They were costly and belonged above all to the great powers. The ram's horn, the shofar, signalled battle.
passages.later: Israel's law warned its kings not to trust in the war horse: ‘the king must not acquire many horses for himself’ (Deuteronomy 17:16).
passages.asks: God delights in an ostrich that looks foolish and runs like the wind. Ask whether you can laugh with God at the strange things he has made. And ask where you have trusted in strength, like the war horse, rather than in the one who gave it.

passages.happening:
“Does the hawk take flight by your understanding and spread his wings toward the south? Does the eagle soar at your command and make his nest on high?” (verses 26-27).

The eagle lives on a cliff, on a rocky crag. From there he spies out food far off. ‘His young ones feast on blood; and where the slain are, there he is’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The word for eagle, nesher, may often mean the griffon vulture, which fits the last verse.

The chapter is arranged mostly in pairs: goat and doe, wild donkey and wild ox, ostrich and horse, hawk and eagle. Each portrait begins with a question to Job and then describes the animal. It ends on a stark image. God's world is not tame, and the speech does not pretend that it is.

When this chapter ends, God will pause and ask Job to reply (40:1-2).
passages.later: The same bird is a picture of strength God gives elsewhere: ‘those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles’ (Isaiah 40:31).
passages.hard:
Why does God speak about animals, ending with an eagle feeding on the slain, to a man grieving his children?

The speech can seem strangely unrelated to Job's pain, and its last image seems harsh. Interpreters have offered several answers. One is that God is enlarging Job's world. Job has measured everything by his own suffering and by whether he was treated justly, and God shows him a creation so vast and varied that no single human life can be its measure. Another is that the wild animals show a world that runs by God's wisdom rather than by human categories of reward and punishment; the eagle feeding on the slain is part of the wild order God sustains, not a moral lesson.

A third reading notes the tenderness in the speech. God watches the goats in labor and counts their months, and he knows when the young leave home. For a man who lost all his children, that attention is not beside the point. The speech does not comfort Job with explanations, but it shows him a God who sees and cares for what no one else sees.
passages.asks: God's world is wild and not tame, and he holds all of it. Ask whether you can trust a God whose ways are larger than you can follow. And ask what it would mean to be seen, as the mountain goats are seen, by him.
